chunks: And with this chain of transmission, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Sa'dan, who raises it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Verily, Allah, the Mighty and High, has not bestowed a bounty upon a servant except that He has made incumbent upon him therein the proof (hujjah) from Allah, the Mighty and High. Therefore, whoever Allah favors by making him strong, his proof upon him is to fulfill what he is obligated to do and to bear with those below him who are weaker than him. And whoever Allah favors by making him wealthy, his proof upon him is his wealth; it is incumbent upon him therein to attend to the poor with his superogatory charity. And whoever Allah favors by making him noble in lineage and handsome in appearance, his proof upon him is that he praises Allah for that and does not arrogate himself over others in withholding the rights of the weak due to his status of nobility and beauty.

key_terms.تَعَهُّدُ الْفُقَرَاءِ: Attending to/caring for the poor, specifically through superogatory charity (nawafil).
key_terms.حُجَّة: Proof or evidence from God, referring to the specific duties or signs that hold a person accountable for a specific blessing.
key_terms.حُقُوقِ الضُّعَفَاءِ: Rights of the weak/poor, referring to their due entitlements that should not be withheld by the privileged.
key_terms.شَرِيفًا فِي نَسَبِهِ: Noble in lineage, referring to high social or familial status.
key_terms.نِعْمَةٍ: Bounty or favor, referring to any blessing bestowed by God upon a servant.

ai.seo_question: What are the specific religious obligations associated with wealth, strength, and status in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq uses this hadith to illustrate the Shia concept of 'Hujjah' as the inherent accountability attached to every divine favor, linking material blessings directly to spiritual duty. It emphasizes that strength, wealth, and lineage are not for domination but for bearing the burdens of the weak, while wealth and status demand active charity and humility to prevent arrogance. This reflects the broader theological principle that God's grace is never gratuitous but always carries a specific covenant of service.
